$comment: How a worker classifies a job's failure, as every worker must classify it: the class it reports on job:fail as failureClass, which the retry rule of specs/src/jobs/retry-cases.json then acts on. A `failure` is described as data: its `name`, where it is one of the failures the worker and its inference drivers declare; `aborted`, where the call was torn down by the one who made it; the HTTP `status` it carries; and the `stopReason` of the reply that could not be read: whichever of those it has. A failure that is a string or null is something thrown that is no failure object at all. `failureClass` is what the worker reports: "deterministic" (the same request cannot succeed a second time, so the retry budget is skipped), "transient" (nothing about the request was judged), or null where the failure is not classified and the field is left off the wire, which the retry rule treats as retryable. Only a failure known to be deterministic is called so: calling a transient failure deterministic halves reliability, where the reverse costs one wasted attempt. The rule is asked in this order and the first part that answers decides. (1) What the worker itself raised: a DeterministicJobError, or any kind of one (a YieldCollapseError is one), is deterministic; an InferenceTimeoutError, the worker's own bound on a model call, is transient. (2) What an inference driver raised for a reply it could not read as the array asked for: a StructuredReadError is deterministic when its stop reason is max_tokens, and with any other stop reason is left unclassified. (3) An abort is transient. An abort is what the language raises when a call is torn down by the one who made it: JavaScript's AbortError, Python's asyncio.CancelledError. A driver reports its library's abort as the language's, and declares none of its own. (4) By status, where the failure carries one as a number: a driver's ProviderStatusError carries the status its provider refused a generation with, and the SDK's failure carries the status a gateway refused with. A status the `job` rule of specs/src/retry/cases.json retries is transient, any other status of 400 or more is deterministic, and a status below 400 decides nothing. (5) Anything else is not classified: a connection that ended or a network failure, whatever the library that reported it calls it. No part of the rule reads the name a provider's library gives a failure: a driver turns what its library raised into the failures above, or passes it on unread. To run a case a runner builds the failure described: for a `name`, the worker's or the driver's own failure of that name, and a runner refuses a name it does not have; for `aborted`, its language's abort; for a description with neither, a plain failure; and it puts the `status` given on whichever it built. TypeScript runs every case in packages/jobs (src/__tests__/failure-class-cases.test.ts) against classifyFailure; a worker in another language runs the same file against its own. Add a case here before changing an implementation.

cases.why: the worker's own mark on a failure it knows cannot succeed a second time: a reply cut off despite the derived budget, a media type with nothing to extract
a yield collapse is a kind of DeterministicJobError: it was measured identical across retries, so a retry is spent for nothing
the worker's own bound on a model call ran out: a stall says nothing about the request
a reply that could not be read because the output budget cut it off: the same text is cut off the same way

a model that finished and still could not be read stays retryable, and unclassified rather than transient: a resumed unit re-cuts the piece at another size, so the next attempt reads different input, which is neither weather nor the same request
an unreadable reply whose stop reason the provider did not state: not provably repeatable, and a server that is really broken deserves its retry budget
only max_tokens says the reply was cut off: any other stop reason leaves an unreadable reply unclassified
an abort: the worker's own bound or shutdown tore the call down, and nothing was judged
an abort is asked about before a status: whatever status rides an abort, no server gave it as a verdict
408 is a timeout, which the job rule retries
429 is the provider saying not now
500 is retried by the job rule: the alternative is discarding paid work
503 is a promise to recover: a driver's ProviderStatusError carries the status its provider refused with
every status from 500 up, a provider's own 529 (overloaded) among them
400 is a rejected request, a provider's as any other: sent again unchanged it is rejected again
401 will be refused again
404: bytes that are not there will not be there on a second identical read
413 is not weather: a payload too large is too large again, though an HTTP client's own rule would retry it
a status below 400 refused nothing, and decides nothing
a status is a number: text that looks like one is not read as one
a failure nothing here recognises, a dropped stream or a network failure for one, carries no status: it stays unclassified and so retryable
what was thrown is text, not a failure object
nothing at all was thrown as the failure
